title: Foundational inference narrative brief
content:
Purpose
This is a compact, internal one-pager to lock down the core narrative we take to product teams and platform buyers when positioning Redwood as the inference layer they choose for production LLM features. It is intentionally concise: one page for alignment, then expanded collateral after sign-off.

Audience (primary)
- Product/ML engineers building customer-facing features where latency, cost, and reliability matter.
- Platform teams standardizing model serving across business units.
- Security/compliance leads evaluating private deployment or auditability.

Core proposition (single-sentence lead)
Redwood provides a production-first inference runtime and control plane that makes deploying LLM features predictable, cost-effective, and safe across hosted, reserved, and private footprints.

Three strategic pillars (how we prove it)
1) Predictable performance at scale — consistent latency and throughput SLOs backed by a runtime that optimizes kernels, batching, and KV/cache behavior for real workloads.
2) Operational control & observability — per-route cost/latency visibility, rollout primitives (canary/A-B/fallback), and tooling to diagnose regressions fast.
3) Deployment flexibility & security — same API/rollout model across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments so teams can start on hosted and safely migrate to isolated capacity without a rewrite.

Why this matters (the buyer problem)
- Modern products can’t tolerate sudden inference cost spikes, unexplained latency regressions, or feature outages caused by model/infra changes.
- Engineering teams don’t want to become full-time ops shops to keep LLM-powered features stable and economical.
- Enterprises require deployment and data controls that general public cloud endpoints don’t consistently satisfy.

Proof points (short bullets we can cite)
- Runtime optimizations: 20–40% lower P99 latency vs baseline for common seq lengths (internal benchmark set).
- Cost controls: templated batching + KV caching reduced token cost ~25% on conversational workloads in pilot customers.
- Portability: single API used in hosted + dedicated installs during two customer migrations without code changes.
- Reliability: built-in fallbacks kept production traffic alive during a regional outage in an early adopter pilot (automatic model variant failover).

Typical buyer scenarios (how prospects frame the problem)
- Fast-growing SaaS: “We want to add chat/assist without our costs doubling or the helpdesk seeing new outages.”
- Regulated customer: “We need private inference with audit trails and KMS integration.”
- Platform team: “Multiple product teams need a standardized serving layer so we can consolidate support.”

Elevator pitches (30s versions)
- For engineers: "Swap in a runtime that treats latency, cost, and reliability as first-class — same SDK, fewer surprises in production."
- For platform/infra: "A unified inference abstraction that scales from shared hosted endpoints to dedicated private clusters, with rollout controls and telemetry you actually use."

Message dos/don’ts
Do: emphasize operational outcomes (SLOs, cost/unit, rollback confidence), talk about concrete tooling (per-route tracing, token-level cost).
Don’t: lead with model metrics or claim model superiority — we sell serving and ops, not model research. Avoid vague ‘AI acceleration’ platitudes without numbers.

Competitive framing (short battle card)
- OpenAI / Anthropic: strongest in simplicity and model quality; weaker on private deployments and tenant-level cost transparency. Lead with our deployment choices and per-token observability.
- Major cloud vendor endpoints: compete on scale/footprint; they lack inference-first runtime optimizations and a consistent managed->dedicated->private migration path. Pitch portability and predictable economics.
- Self-hosted inference runtimes: good on control but expensive to implement/operate; Redwood reduces build+run effort with a pre-integrated control plane and rollout tooling.

Key objections and rebuttals
- "We can control costs by ourselves": point to engineering effort required and show cost comparisons from pilot customers plus the templates we provide to automate batching/cache.
- "We’re already on cloud provider endpoints": highlight migration pain, blind spots in cost telemetry, and the lack of cross-environment rollout primitives.
- "We need strict data controls/air-gapped": describe Redwood Private options (customer-managed control plane, KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs) and reference recent compliance engagements.

Suggested hero lines / variants for web/lead gen
- "Reliable inference, without the ops burden."
- "Ship LLM features that behave in production."
- "Same API. Any deployment. Predictable costs."

Open questions / items to resolve before finalizing collateral
- Can we centralize and agree on 2–3 benchmark slices (conversational, summarization, embeddings) and canonical numbers for collateral? (Action: eng applied-ml to produce repeatable runs; Jira INF-7823)
- Exact phrasing for Private offering (legal review on claims around on-prem/air-gap).
- Customer quotes: who can we cite from pilots? (Sales to follow up.)

Next steps (immediate)
- Align with Applied ML to lock benchmark numbers (owner: Diego).
- Product to confirm GA feature list for rollout controls and telemetry (owner: Zara).
- Draft external one-pager and two-sentence elevator for website; iterate with comms.

Notes / working fragments (leave as-is for context)
- Avoid over-indexing on model names; customers care less about the model upstream and more about how latency/cost/availability land in their stack.
- Consider a short technical diagram for ops docs: request flow -> smart router -> runtime (batch/cache) -> telemetry/fallthrough.
- Retain language that supports both technical buyers and security/compliance stakeholders.

Document history
- v0.1 initial draft 2025-11-03 (Maya)
- v0.2 added proof points and battlecard 2026-01-14 (Liam)
- v0.3 updated benchmarks placeholder and open Qs 2026-03-09 (Diego)

End of brief.
